summary: Applies the opportunistic security idea from RFC 7435 to the Real-time Transport Protocol. It lets endpoints use encrypted media when both sides support it, and fall back to unencrypted media when they do not, without needing new SDP extensions. It is meant as a transitional approach and works with any SRTP key management.

eli5.summary: It is like whispering when the other person can hear whispers, and speaking normally when they cannot. Calls use secret mode if both sides can, and still connect if not.

when should you use osrtp vs mandatory encryption
subtitle: Encrypted media calls with optional encryption support.

tldr.problem: Real-time communications want to use encryption when both endpoints support it, but still need to work when encryption support is unknown or unavailable.
tldr.mechanism: OSRTP allows endpoints to offer encrypted media using SRTP alongside regular RTP in a single offer, using standard SDP attributes. The answerer chooses to use encryption if it supports it, or falls back to unencrypted media.
tldr.outcome: Calls automatically get encrypted media when possible without requiring new SDP extensions or SIP changes. This enables incremental migration of existing deployments to full encryption.

today: RFC 8643 is Informational and remains in use by endpoint implementers building transitional systems. It is not a standards-track protocol, so it does not define network requirements, only guidance for migration.

sections.title: Opportunistic Security for Real-time Media
sections.content:
Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries audio and video between applications, but by default it sends media without encryption. OSRTP applies the idea of opportunistic security from RFC 7435 to RTP, allowing both ends to use encrypted media (SRTP) when both support it, and to fall back to unencrypted RTP when one side does not.

The key insight is that OSRTP works with existing RTP profiles and SDP attributes—it needs no new extensions or special negotiation. An offerer includes SRTP key material (such as a DTLS fingerprint or crypto key) in a normal RTP/AVP offer, signaling support for opportunistic secure media. If the answerer sees these SRTP attributes and supports encryption, it includes them in the reply and both sides use SRTP. If the answerer does not include them, the call uses standard RTP.

This is most useful as a transitional tool: for existing deployments migrating from plain RTP to SRTP, OSRTP provides a middle ground that does not break compatibility with peers that do not yet support encryption.
sections.eli5: Your phone says "I can talk in secret or normal mode." If the other phone says "I can too," you both use secrets. If they say nothing about secrets, you just talk normally.

sections.title: SDP Offer and Answer
sections.content:
OSRTP relies on the Session Description Protocol to negotiate encryption. An initial OSRTP offer includes SRTP keying attributes—such as fingerprints (from DTLS-SRTP), crypto keys (from SDP Security Descriptions), or ZRTP hashes—inside an SDP media section marked with the standard RTP/AVP or RTP/AVPF profile, not a secure profile.

To accept OSRTP, an answerer replies with SRTP keying attributes matching one of those offered. The answerer MUST NOT pick attributes from more than one key management method, even if the offer contained several. If the answerer includes no SRTP attributes at all, the media session proceeds with plain RTP.

If SRTP key agreement fails after either side commits to it, the media session MUST fail. This means that once encryption is negotiated, both sides must successfully establish it or the call drops; the protocol does not fall back to plain RTP mid-session.
sections.eli5: Your offer lists your secret codes. The other person picks one and sends it back. You both use it, or you both give up and talk plainly.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
OSRTP is weaker than mandatory SRTP, because it relaxes authentication requirements when encryption is optional. For example, DTLS-SRTP with OSRTP does not require the signaling channel to be authenticated, so a man-in-the-middle could intercept and modify the SDP offer. However, because OSRTP is intended only for scenarios where encryption support is unknown and not required, this trade-off is deliberate.

When OSRTP is used with SDP Security Descriptions (RFC 4568), the RFC requires that messages carrying SRTP keys be encrypted. However, it is common for SIP proxies to inspect SDP, and OSRTP acknowledges that such intermediaries may see the SRTP keys. This risk is accepted to enable opportunistic encryption without strong signaling security.

Most importantly, OSRTP MUST NOT be used when it is known that both endpoints support SRTP or when encryption is mandatory. In those cases, a secure RTP profile (SAVP or SAVPF) MUST be used in the offer instead. OSRTP is only for the case where encryption support is unknown in advance.
sections.eli5: Opportunistic encryption is weaker than real encryption because someone could trick you into not using it. But it is only meant when you do not know if the other person can use secrets at all. If you know they can, you should demand secrets.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
One major advantage of OSRTP is that it works with all existing SRTP key management approaches—DTLS-SRTP, SDP Security Descriptions (crypto keys), and ZRTP—without picking a favorite or requiring changes to any of them.

OSRTP is fully backward compatible. An endpoint that implements only plain RTP will ignore the SRTP attributes in an OSRTP offer and reply with an answer that omits them, leaving the media unencrypted. An endpoint that implements only SRTP (using a secure RTP profile) will not recognize an OSRTP offer and either reject it or ignore the offer, so no media negotiation occurs on that offer. This means OSRTP can be deployed in systems that speak only RTP or only SRTP without breaking their ability to interoperate with OSRTP endpoints.
sections.eli5: Old phones that only know plain talking ignore the secret offer and talk plainly. Old phones that only know secrets reject the offer. OSRTP phones understand both, so they get along with everyone.
